When halogenated organics (compounds containing halogens like chlorine, bromine, etc.) are mixed with cyanides (like sodium cyanide or potassium cyanide), a dangerous chemical reaction can occur. In this reaction, the acidic nature of many halogenated compounds can react with cyanide salts to produce hydrogen cyanide (HCN), which is a highly toxic gas. 

The reaction typically follows this pattern:
- Halogenated organic compounds can act as acids
- Cyanide salts (like NaCN) are bases
- When mixed, an acid-base reaction can occur
- This reaction produces hydrogen cyanide gas (HCN), which is extremely toxic

Therefore, the primary hazard when halogenated organics are mixed with cyanides is the generation of toxic gas (hydrogen cyanide).
